passages.text: If he desires “the fat mountain,” to whom do all things belong? If he lies, who then tells the truth? If he dwells in a tent, who then is uncontainable? If he longs for fat-smoke and sacrifices and sacrificial victims and libations, who then needs nothing, and who is holy, and who is pure, and who is perfect? If he delights in lamps and lampstands, who then set the luminaries in heaven? If he is present in thick gloom and darkness and tempest and smoke, who then, being light, illuminates the greatest age? If he approaches with trumpets and loud cries and missiles and arrows, who then is the calm awaited by all? If he himself loves wars, who then desires peace? If he himself “creates” “the evils,” who then fashions good things? If he himself is without affection, who then loves humanity? If he himself is not faithful concerning what he promises, who then will be trusted? If he himself loves wicked people and adulterers and murderers, who then will be a just judge? If he himself “changes his mind,” who then is steadfast? If he himself chooses evil people, who then welcomes good people?

lexical_decisions.rationale: πῖον literally describes something fat or rich and may imply a fertile or luxuriant mountain; the concrete “fat” image is retained because the phrase is quoted.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to whom do all things belong
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally “and whose are all things?” the question challenges the attribution of desire to the one who owns everything.
The adjective denotes one who cannot be contained, confined, or accommodated within a place.
κνίση denotes the greasy smoke or savor rising from burning fat; the compact rendering preserves both the material and sacrificial imagery.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κνίσης καὶ θυσιῶν καὶ θυμάτων καὶ προσχύσεων
lexical_decisions.chosen: fat-smoke and sacrifices and sacrificial victims and libations
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated conjunctions and the distinction between sacrifices, victims, and poured offerings are retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐν γνόφῳ καὶ σκότῳ καὶ θυέλλῃ καὶ καπνῷ σύνεστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: is present in thick gloom and darkness and tempest and smoke
lexical_decisions.rationale: The locative ἐν governs all four atmospheric nouns, while σύνεστιν means “is with” or “is present.” “Is present in” preserves the setting expressed by ἐν and avoids conflating σύνεστιν with the earlier οἰκεῖ, “dwells.”
αἰών may denote an age, eternity, or a world-order. “Age” is the most direct rendering, while “the greatest world” remains a possible contextual interpretation.
βολίδες are thrown projectiles or bolts, while τοξεύματα are things shot from a bow; the two images are kept distinct.
προσδόκιμος means expected or awaited, and τῶν ὅλων can refer either to everyone or collectively to all things.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ „τὰ κακὰ“ αὐτὸς „κτίζει“, καὶ τίς ἀγαθὰ δημιουργεῖ;
lexical_decisions.chosen: If he himself “creates” “the evils,” who then fashions good things?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied edition separately marks both τὰ κακὰ and κτίζει as quoted expressions; the English preserves both sets of quotation marks while adopting natural English word order.
The adjective denotes absence of natural or familial affection; “unloving” is a broader alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: If he himself “changes his mind,” who then is steadfast?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb may also mean “regrets,” but the contrast with βέβαιος, one who is stable or steadfast, favors “changes his mind”; the quotation marking in the supplied edition is preserved.
The verb can mean admits, receives, or accepts; “welcomes” provides a natural contrast with choosing evil people.
